title: Umar at Jerusalem
hookLine: Umar receives Jerusalem's surrender, and tradition says he prayed outside the church so it would stay a church

lines: TIME TO PRAY, INSIDE A CHURCH.
cards: It's time to pray, and the leader of the believers is standing inside a church. Not just any church: the great church in Jerusalem that Christians built over the place where they remember Christ's tomb.
The city has just surrendered. The patriarch who handed it over is beside him. And Umar, the story goes, is asked to pray right there, inside.
He says no. Today: Umar at Jerusalem, and why, as the story is told, he stepped outside.

teach.b: First, the frame. The Qur'an and hadith don't tell this story. It comes from later chroniclers, one of them a Christian patriarch of Alexandria, and Muslims and Christians have both retold it.
It is tradition, not scripture. Jerusalem's patriarch, Sophronius, agreed to surrender the city, but only to the caliph himself. So Umar came.

The histories preserve a covenant of safety for the people of the city, which in its usual form promises them their lives, their property and their churches: the churches would not be lived in, torn down or reduced.
The versions of that document differ, and scholars debate its wording. Then the story. While Umar was being shown the Church of the Resurrection, the time of prayer came.
The patriarch invited him to pray where he stood. Umar declined.

teach.h: IF I PRAY HERE, THEY WILL TAKE IT.
teach.b: If I pray here, he is reported to have said, the Muslims after me will take it, saying: Umar prayed here.

teach.h: HE PRAYED ON THE STEPS OUTSIDE.
teach.b: So he went out and prayed on the steps outside, alone.

Tradition places a mosque named for him near that spot, and the church still stands as a church. The man with every power to take the building chose a smaller thing: to protect it from his own followers' devotion to him.
He knew his prayer would become a claim.

The Qur'an itself names cloisters, churches, synagogues and mosques together as places where God's name is remembered much, places it says would have been pulled down if God did not check one people by another.

how: Muslims and Christians in Jerusalem both retell the story of Umar praying outside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and a mosque named for Umar stands nearby.

games.q: you're Umar, inside the great church of Jerusalem. it's time to pray, and the patriarch invites you to pray where you stand. what do you do?
o: go out and pray on the steps outside.
skip the prayer until you've left the city.
games.why: the story says he went outside, so that no one after him could claim the church because Umar prayed in it.

practice: Bring to mind a place that's holy to someone else: a church, a temple, a synagogue, a gurdwara, a grave, a corner of a friend's home where they pray.
Picture yourself at its door, and ask what it would mean to honor it on its own terms: shoes off, a lowered voice, no photo.

wordCard.voice: Al-Quds, the holy, Jerusalem's Arabic name: the city where Umar, the caliph, received its surrender and stepped outside a church to pray so it would stay a church. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the holy, the Arabic name for Jerusalem.

carryVoice: Your line: he prayed outside. So a church could stay a church. That's day eight hundred seventy-three.
